name: The Wodanseiken

location.address: Wolfhezerheide nature reserve, south of Wolfheze; reached from the parking area at Oude Kloosterweg/Wolfhezerweg near the Fletcher hotel

access: Free. Public nature reserve owned by Natuurmonumenten, reached via a marked path from the Oude Kloosterweg/Wolfhezerweg parking area, roughly a 5-minute walk.
transport: Wolfheze railway station, then about 2 km on the signed Wodanroute walking path.
verify_notes: A named group of (bomenbieb says four, Wikipedia describes several) gnarled oaks in a former heathland along the Wolfhezerbeek, now surrounded by mixed forest. Two independent sources agree: planted/germinated shortly after the 1550 digging of the Wolfhezerbeek stream channel, age variously given as 400-600 years (nl.wikipedia) or 450-500 years (bomenbieb); both are estimates, not documented plantings, so keep the range broad. Largest specimen: 525 cm girth, 22 m tall (bomenbieb). Named around 1850 by landscape painters Johannes Warnardus and Gerard Bilders (the 'Oosterbeekse School'), who met there at night; J.J. Cremer painted them in 1849; first named documentation from 1865. Folklore ties the name to the god Wodan. Wikipedia notes groundwater has dropped 1-2 m over the last century from water extraction and 'a number of trees did not survive' -- so not every original oak in the group is still standing, but the site and named survivors are. location_precision approximate because the coordinate marks the general grove rather than one single trunk; it is a compact, signed viewpoint (the 'Wodanroute' hiking route is built around it), so treat as one collectible ensemble entry, not several. Girth/height are for the single most prominent specimen per bomenbieb; other trees in the group are smaller.

name: Philemon

location.address: Former Beekhuizen estate, between Hotel Beekhuizen and the path down to the Beekhuizerbeek waterfall, Velp

access: Free. Public grounds of the former Beekhuizen estate (part of Nationaal Park Veluwezoom), on the signed 'Ommetje Beekhuizen' walking route beside Hotel Beekhuizen.
transport: From Velp or Arnhem, bus toward Rozendaal/Beekhuizen, then a short walk on the estate paths.
verify_notes: IMPORTANT: this was a named PAIR, Philemon and Baucis (after Ovid's hospitable elderly couple who were turned into an oak and a linden), but Baucis blew down in storm Ciaran at the end of 2023 -- confirmed by two independent, dated local news reports (Regiobode Dec 2025, rheden.nieuws.nl), both describing a sapling grown from a Baucis acorn (kept by Joris Hellevoort of the Bomenstichting since 2020) being planted on almost the same spot on 8 December 2025, fenced against wildlife. Baucis is therefore DEAD and must not ship as a living entry (see blocked note in leads file); bomenbieb.nl's own vitality field still wrongly says Baucis is alive, a stale-register case worth flagging generally. Only PHILEMON ships here. No source explicitly states in one sentence that Philemon still stands, but every account discusses only Baucis's fall and replacement, never mentions Philemon being lost, and bomenbieb (checked 2026-09) still lists it as alive -- flagged rather than fully confirmed for that reason. Philemon is multi-stemmed, girth about 6 m, 23 m tall, estimated 300-500 years old (bomenbieb), planted 1520-1720. First documented mention of the pair is from 1820; the site appears in a 1930s-40s Gelders Archief photograph. One of the oldest trees in Rheden municipality and a genuine local landmark, the subject of repeated local press coverage over the storm loss and replacement. Girth is for Philemon specifically per bomenbieb; do not confuse with Baucis's figures (5 m girth, 24 m, now dead).

name: The Thousand-Year Oak of Doornenburg
age_estimate: several hundred years (popularly, but not literally, called 'the thousand-year oak')

location.address: Kerkstraat 27, 6686 BS Doornenburg (south side of Kasteel Doornenburg)

access: Free, no castle ticket needed. A path runs from the small free car park at Kasteel Doornenburg straight to the tree, with a bench and an ANWB information sign beside it.
transport: Doornenburg village; nearest station is Zevenaar or Arnhem, then bus/bike into the village and a short walk to the castle.
verify_notes: Skeptical read of the name: despite being called the 'thousand-year oak' and locally claimed on a municipal sign as the oldest oak in the Netherlands, no source supports a literal 1000-year age. The castle's own page (kasteeldoornenburg.nl) says the tree was 300-400 years old by expert estimate in the early 19th century, implying roughly 500-600+ years now; 2013 wood/growth-ring sampling (reported by Vroege Vogels/BNNVARA and De Erfgoedstem) put it at 400-650 years; monumentaltrees.com (cross-check only) gives 522 plus/minus 150 years. So treat the age as several hundred years, broad range, never as 1000. First written mention of a tree here is from 1376, which is corroborating but not itself an age (a document can name an old tree without dating it). Trunk is completely hollow, one side open and closed off with a steel gate/fence against fire and carving; two thick hollow stubs may be remnants of old pollarding. Circumference 656 cm per the castle's own 2021 measurement (bomenbieb gives an older 565 cm figure; the castle's page also notes growth of 2-5 cm/year 2006-2021, which is itself evidence of continued life). Height 15 m (measured 2013). Local nicknames: Den Ouden Eik, Uiverboom/Uivereik (stork tree), for at least two centuries. There is a live, ongoing rival claim from Den Hout's Heilige Eik (see that entry, candidate 4 of this batch) for 'oldest tree in the Netherlands' -- do not let either page assert the superlative as settled fact; per hard rule 8 a superlative is fine to state as believed but our own two pages must not both claim the exact same crown outright.

name: The Heilige Eik (Holy Oak) of Den Hout
age_estimate: several centuries; a forester who studied it argues it may be the oldest living oak in the Netherlands, planted around 1250

location.address: Vrachelsestraat, at the corner with Achterstraat, Den Hout

access: Free. Stands at an ordinary road junction between the hamlet of Vrachelen and the village of Den Hout, with its own marker sign; visible and reachable from public roads at all times.
transport: Den Hout village, near Oosterhout; nearest station Oosterhout, then bus or bike to the village.
verify_notes: Genuine conflicting age readings across sources, recorded rather than picked: nl.wikipedia says most experts think the current tree was planted in the 16th century on the site of an earlier medieval 'Heilige Eik' (first mentioned in a land deed of 1353); but Joris Hellevoort, a forester with Het Utrechts Landschap who has studied it, argues it is one continuous tree planted around 1250, making it roughly 750-770 years old and possibly the oldest living oak in the Netherlands (widely covered: NOS national news, Omroep Brabant, BredaNu, Erfgoed Brabant). Omroep Brabant's piece (dated by its own byline to March 2026, with an update note from mid-2024) confirms it is alive with a healthy, densely leafed crown 'every summer', and that it came second in a regional 'Tree of the Year' contest. Girth about 4 m, height about 13 m (bomenbieb, Omroep Brabant agree). The trunk is hollowed by an old lightning strike (roughly two centuries ago per Omroep Brabant) and open on one side; only one living branch now forms the crown. The name reflects a likely pre-Christian tree-shrine origin on the same spot, and the tree appears on the Oosterhout mayoral chain of office. Oosterhout municipality has been installing protective measures (a metal support/stut) to keep it from breaking in high wind, per municipal and local-news coverage. NOTE ON SUPERLATIVE: this tree and the Thousand-Year Oak of Doornenburg (candidate 3 of this batch) are both locally promoted as 'the oldest oak/tree in the Netherlands'. Both claims are real, sourced and disputed, so record both entries with their claim attributed to its own source, and do not let both of our own pages assert the same crown as fact (hard rule 8).

name: The Gebodenlinde of Hilvarenbeek

location.address: Vrijthof (village square), Hilvarenbeek, next to the church

access: Free. Stands in the open village square (Vrijthof) beside the church, water pump and bandstand, with a bench beneath it; fully public at all times.
transport: Hilvarenbeek village centre; nearest station Tilburg, then bus into the village.
verify_notes: A 'gebodenlinde' (proclamation lime): the schepenen (aldermen) of Hilvarenbeek announced village decrees under this tree and it also sheltered the linen market and served as a courthouse tree, per the local heemkundige kring (heritage society)'s own plaque text and bomenbieb. A document dated 22 April 1676 records that a young lime had recently been planted on the Vrijthof, replacing an earlier lime that died in 1675; bomenbieb notes some uncertainty over whether today's tree is that 1676 planting or a 1704 replacement, so the age given is broad on purpose. Girth 621 cm, height 23 m (bomenbieb). Heavy limbs were given structural support in 1974. Omroep Brabant (regional broadcaster) reported the municipality is currently studying how to improve the tree's growing conditions (more root space, air and water) to keep this 300-plus-year-old tree healthy, which is itself a form of confirmation it is alive and being actively managed today.

name: Adam en Eva of Stoutenburg
access: Free to view, not free to enter. The two oaks stand on the private Stoutenburg estate behind a closed gate but are visible from the public road (Stoutenburgerlaan); the pin marks the roadside viewing point, not the trunks.
transport: Leusden/Amersfoort area; nearest station Amersfoort, then bus or bike towards Stoutenburg.
verify_notes: A named pair of ancient oaks on the grounds of the 13th-century Landgoed Stoutenburg, ranked by the Bomenstichting (Dutch Tree Foundation) as 'Bomen van Ereklasse' (champion class) and the second-most notable tree pair in Utrecht province. Local tradition (repeated by bomenbieb and by erfgoedstem.nl, a regional heritage-news site) says they were planted in memory of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, the Land's Advocate who held the estate from 1615 until his execution in 1619 -- but erfgoedstem is explicit this is a legend, not a documented planting: 'whether the trees truly originate from that era remains unknown', and the Bomenstichting itself only calls an age over 350 years 'plausible'. Do not present the Oldenbarnevelt connection as fact; it is a good anecdote clearly labelled as tradition. Thickest of the two ('Adam' per the search summary, treat as approximate) has a girth around 6.60 m. Both trees are heavily damaged and have needed repeated arboricultural intervention (steel cable bracing, ground reinforcement, propping a low major limb), carried out by tree-care firm Copijn together with Utrechts Landschap, which also confirms they are actively managed and alive today. bomenbieb notes the trees stand behind a closed gate but are visible from the road, so this ships as a view-only entry per the hard-rule-10 exception: honest about the closed gate, pin at the roadside rather than the trunks.

name: The Kroezeboom of Fleringen
age_estimate: roughly 400 to 500 years; some local claims go much higher but are not well supported

location.address: Lansinkweg, on the Fleringer Es between Tubbergen and Fleringen, beside the chapel

access: Free. Public site with a marked parking area on the Jan van Arkelweg and a signed, roughly 5-minute walk to the tree; an unpaved path runs alongside it. A cast-iron fence protects the trunk itself, so visitors view rather than touch it.
transport: Nearest station Almelo, then bus toward Tubbergen/Fleringen and a walk from the village.
verify_notes: A 'kroezeboom' (from the Twente/Achterhoek tradition of boundary and gathering oaks, see nl.wikipedia's 'Kroezeboom' article): likely planted 1500-1600 as a boundary marker (a 'loakboom') between fields on the Fleringer Es, and later a site where border disputes were settled. During the Reformation, Catholics held secret Mass here until roughly 1730 at a small field chapel ('hilligen huesken') beside the tree; the current small timber-framed chapel (replacing a 1944 neo-Gothic one) has been a gathering site for Catholic and peace-movement meetings since 1970, per VisitOost. The Sint Pancratius parish of Tubbergen has owned the site since 1916. Girth 725 cm (VisitOost); some sources call this the oldest summer oak in the Netherlands and speculate it could be 700-1000 years old, but the better-supported estimate (bomenbieb, consistent with a 1500-1600 planting) is 400-500 years, so the age is recorded conservatively and the wilder claim is not repeated as fact. Received arborist treatment (steel cables/supports) under Jorn Copijn in the 1960s-70s, still visible. NOTE ON SUPERLATIVE: at least three trees in this batch (this one, the Thousand-Year Oak of Doornenburg, and the Heilige Eik of Den Hout) are locally promoted as 'the oldest tree/oak in the Netherlands'. All three claims are real and locally sourced but mutually exclusive; do not let more than one of our pages assert the crown as settled fact (hard rule 8).

name: The Pollard Oaks of the Koningstafel
age_estimate: documented since at least 1830; local tradition holds them considerably older

location.address: West side of the Koningstafel plateau, Grebbeberg, near Rhenen

access: Free. Public heritage site managed by Utrechts Landschap on the Grebbeberg, with waymarked walking and cycling routes; the plateau is also a WWII memorial site (Slag om de Grebbeberg, May 1940) and is visited routinely.
transport: Rhenen railway station, then a signed walk up the Grebbeberg (roughly 25-30 minutes).
verify_notes: A cluster of low-pollarded ('geknot') oaks on the west side of the Koningstafel, an elevated plateau on the Grebbeberg overlooking the Rhine, inside the Heimenberg ring-wall earthwork, one of the oldest and largest defensive structures in the Netherlands (7th century, per grebbeberg.nl). Some of the trees stand in circular groupings that make individual dating hard. Ages conflict between sources and both are recorded rather than picked: bomenbieb gives a broad planting band of 1200-1750, while grebbeberg.nl says the pollards are documented from at least 1830 and 'possibly much older'. Treat 1830 as the safe floor and the earlier dates as tradition. The plateau took its name 'King's Table' in the 17th century after the exiled Frederick V of the Palatinate reportedly used it for hunting feasts and had a large stone table placed there; this is a place-name legend, not evidence about the trees' age. This is a compact ensemble entry (a named cluster at one viewpoint), not a single named specimen; no girth or height figures were found in the sources checked. Ownership/management by Utrechts Landschap.

name: The Lodewijkslinde of Vorden

location.address: De Horsterkamp 14, Vorden, near the coach house of Kasteel Vorden

access: Free. On the grounds of Landgoed Vorden, managed by Geldersch Landschap en Kasteelen, open to walkers with a car park on site; the castle building itself is now a private wedding/hotel venue, but the estate grounds around it are public.
transport: Within walking distance of Vorden railway station (per the estate's own management, GLK).
verify_notes: Presumably planted 1622-1623 (bomenbieb); named for a local legend that French king Louis XIV rested under it in 1672 during the French invasion of the Dutch Republic -- this is tradition, not a documented fact about the specific tree, and should be told as legend. First pictorial evidence is a watercolour from the first half of the 19th century and a painting from 1874, which corroborates the tree's age but not the Louis XIV story specifically. Girth about 5.5 m (bomenbieb and GLK, the estate's own trust, agree), originally reached about 30 m tall but lost its main stem and two large limbs to wood rot in 2002; height now roughly 13 m per bomenbieb. Stands near a second monumental tree on the same estate, the 'Dikke Eik' (Fat Oak, girth almost 7 m, not one of our 12 candidates), which a writer could mention as a nearby second stop on the same estate walk.

name: The Dorpslinde of Nuenen
access: Free. Stands in the open on Nuenen's village green (de Berg), protected by an iron fence since 1889 but fully visible and reachable by the public at all times.
transport: Nuenen village centre; nearest station Eindhoven, then bus into the village.
verify_notes: The thickest summer/large-leaved lime in the Netherlands (bomenbieb, VisitBrabant), a rare species for the region, planted roughly 1625-1650 and first recorded in the burgemeester's accounts of 1702; a 'gerechtslinde' (justice lime) under which judgments and announcements were historically made. Girth 660 cm. In 1994 the upper crown had to be removed after a tinder-fungus (Fomes fomentarius) infection, leaving a pergola-like hollow shell; age is estimated from growth rings still visible in that hollow trunk and in a surviving thick branch. Good story detail, confirmed by more than one source: on 28 December 2019, exactly 25 years after the crown removal, former 'carnival princes' of the Nuenen carnival club De Dwersklippels planted a new summer linden sapling inside the ancient hollow trunk as a prank; the mayor later ruled by official proclamation that the new tree could stay, on condition the pranksters organise a small remembrance ceremony at the tree every 28 December. The centuries-old original trunk is what remains alive and is the entry here; the sapling inside it is a separate, recent addition and should be described as such, not conflated with the tree's age. CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, per the brief: tourism copy (Van Gogh Village Nuenen's own walking routes, VisitBrabant) repeats that 'Vincent van Gogh saw this tree' during his 1883-1885 Nuenen years, since it stands on the village's central square which he painted and walked daily, but no source found here cites a specific letter, sketch or painting naming this tree. Treat the Van Gogh link as plausible local tradition tied to his residence, not a documented fact, and say so if used.

name: The Linde van Sambeek

location.address: Grotestraat 93, Sambeek (on the through-road in the south of the village)

access: Free. Stands beside the public through-road at the south end of Sambeek village; reachable at any time.
transport: Sambeek village, near Boxmeer; nearest station Boxmeer, then bus or bike into the village.
verify_notes: The thickest and, by local claim, oldest lime tree in the Netherlands, registered in the Landelijk Register van Monumentale Bomen (monument #1679463 per nl.wikipedia). Girth 7.97 m measured in 2004; height about 23 m; exact age impossible to pin down because the trunk is hollow, so the 350-500 year estimate is the sources' own honest range. Originally a three-tiered ceremonial lime, it lost its tiers in an 1884 storm and nearly its whole crown in a second storm in 1901, after which it was expected to die but instead resprouted: a new stem grew from the old root system inside the hollow trunk and now has its own girth of about 2.5 m, itself forming part of today's crown. Restored again in 1973-74 (municipal funding, cable anchors, iron trunk supports, root-zone treatment). Declared a 'World Tree' in 2015 by Stichting Wereldboom and pruned under their guidance. Recent and strong evidence of continued life and civic care: in 2025 the municipality of Land van Cuijk decided to realign and narrow the road past the tree specifically to give its roots more space and protect it, reported in local coverage. Good candidate for 'confirmed alive' given multiple points of recent, dated municipal and press attention.
